headline: New England groups file fresh challenge to birthright citizenship order
dek: ACLU affiliates in Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts joined a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump's August order, while an earlier injunction remains in place.
body: A new federal lawsuit led in part by the ACLU of Maine is asking a Washington, D.C., court to block the Trump administration's latest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship. The case, Nathan v. Trump, was filed Sept. 28 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, according to the public docket. The coalition includes the national ACLU, ACLU affiliates in Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and the District of Columbia, the Legal Defense Fund, the Asian Law Caucus and the Democracy Defenders Fund. The groups say the order violates the Constitution and federal citizenship law; those are allegations in a newly filed complaint, not a ruling by the court (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2026cv03377/297026).

The lawsuit targets Executive Order 14418, which President Donald Trump signed Aug. 6 and the Federal Register published Aug. 11. The order directs federal agencies not to issue documents recognizing U.S. citizenship, or accept state and local documents purporting to recognize it, when neither parent is a U.S. citizen and specified conditions apply. Those conditions include a parent classified as an alien enemy, certain foreign-government or international-organization employees, and a parent alleged to have used a commercial transaction or fraud to obtain citizenship. The order also addresses some births in U.S. territories where federal law does not confer citizenship (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/eo-14418.pdf).

The filing's practical reach is broader than the phrase “birth tourism” often used in public debate. The order specifically refers to arrangements in which a parent pays to ensure that a mother is in the United States to give birth or pays a surrogate who is in the country. It also gives agencies enforcement responsibilities, including the State Department, Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security and Social Security Administration. If implemented, those instructions could affect how families obtain or use federal citizenship documentation, although the order's ultimate legal effect is now being contested in court.

The plaintiffs' legal theory relies on the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause and the federal statute that codifies birthright citizenship. The complaint cites the Supreme Court's 1898 decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark and says the Constitution does not allow the president to create new exceptions by executive order. The filing also points to the Supreme Court's June decision in Trump v. Barbara, which the ACLU says rejected the administration's earlier, broader order. The Associated Press separately reported that the Supreme Court struck down that earlier attempt before the administration issued the narrower August order (https://www.aclumaine.org/app/uploads/2026/09/NATHAN-v.-TRUMP-Complaint.pdf; https://apnews.com/article/trump-again-tries-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship-after-supreme-court-ruling-494add8239eb1c0c9f4ccb45db03f1f0).

For New England, the case places legal organizations from three states in the next phase of the fight. ACLU of Maine Legal Director Carol Garvan is quoted in the group's announcement as arguing that the Supreme Court's decision prevents the president or Congress from ending birthright citizenship. ACLU affiliates are advocacy organizations, not state governments, so Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts are not plaintiffs as states in this case. The regional connection is instead the participation of groups that represent or organize around immigrant-rights issues in those states (https://www.aclumaine.org/press-releases/immigrants-rights-advocates-file-federal-lawsuit-challenging-new-trump-birthright-citizenship-executive-order/).

The new D.C. case follows a separate court fight over the same August order. The Associated Press reported that U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland issued a preliminary injunction on Sept. 2 while a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups proceeds. Maine Public also reported that the Maryland judge temporarily paused the order and described it as almost certainly unconstitutional. That injunction is separate from Nathan v. Trump; it does not mean the new case has already been decided (https://apnews.com/article/69de0a404602a6e648b35f6a852c833d; https://www.mainepublic.org/immigration/2026-09-28/aclu-of-maine-sues-trump-administration-over-latest-attempt-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship).

The public D.C. docket lists the Sept. 28 complaint and motions asking the court to let the plaintiffs proceed under pseudonyms and file later exhibits under seal. It did not list a merits ruling as of the docket's Sept. 28 retrieval date. The next important steps will be the government's response and any decision on a request for preliminary relief. Until then, the complaint records the challengers' claims, the executive order records the administration's policy, and the courts—not either side in the lawsuit—will determine whether the new restrictions can be enforced.
